posts.title: Government Agencies Got Hit. Here’s What It Means for You.
posts.description: If you saw the headlines this week, you might be thinking that if the government can’t keep hackers out, what chance do you have? That’s a fair question. Take a breath, because the answer is better than it sounds. What happened In about a week, we heard about the FBI investigating an apparent breach of its national crime database , an unclassified intelligence system used by the CIA being broken into, Treasury’s financial crimes bureau confirming unauthorized access to some systems, and a report that hackers got into an Air Force cloud platform . A lot is still unknown. We don’t have the full story on who did it or what was taken, and I haven’t seen anything official saying these are connected. Why it isn’t a reason to give up Government agencies are some of the biggest targets in the world. They run huge numbers of systems, and the people going after them can be patient and well funded. posts.title: Cyber Monday: Five Checks Before You Click Buy
posts.description: Cyber Monday is built to make you move fast. Scammers like that. Before you click buy, take one minute and run these five checks. Five checks Type the address yourself. Scammers buy search ads that can sit at the very top of your results. The FTC warned about this on November 19 . Look up a store you do not know. Search its name with “scam” or “complaint” before you give it a card number. Pay with a credit card when you can. If the order never shows, you can dispute the charge . Walk away from odd payment demands. Gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto to buy a sweater? No. Do not tap the link in a surprise delivery text . Open the carrier’s app or site yourself and check there. If you already got hit Call your card company or bank now, using the number on the back of the card. Change the password if you typed one into that site, and anywhere else you reused it. Then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov , and to the FBI at ic3.gov if you lost money. posts.title: Five Failures in Ten Days: Coordinated Attack or Brittle Systems?
posts.description: Between November 8 and November 16, 2026, Nvidia’s CEO resigned over an alleged Chinese intelligence link. Microsoft 365 went down worldwide. The FAA grounded every flight in the country. Chase and other big banks had login problems. And United Airlines delayed departures over a system failure. That many big failures in one stretch feels like a pattern, and a lot of people are asking whether it was one attack. This post goes through each event: what officials say caused it, what is still unconfirmed, and what the events actually have in common. Short version: as of November 16, no investigator has tied any of these to a cyberattack or to each other. Most of the final root-cause reports are not out yet. M y Take: They cyber incident with Microsoft was a big one for me, that had me thinking. Is this an attacked or how much testing should you do before your IT team introduce’s new changes to your system?
